text.p: Zurich Group expressed confidence that group profits would show double-digit growth in 1997 and executives said the insurance giant was keen on expanding further, particularly in asset management.
"Unless faced with exceptional events, we expect to achieve another good overall result for the 1997 financial year," the life and non-life insurance group said in its annual report.
"A good result must be double digit growth...I can't say more, but I am confident that we will have a good result (in 1997)," Zurich's chairman Rolf Hueppi told a news conference.
He characterised the average growth rate of the last five years, which was around 21 percent, as "very good" growth.
Zurich Group in April reported that its 1996 net profit rose 30 percent to 1.138 billion Swiss francs ($821.5 million) and gross insurance premiums were up by 20.5 percent to 31.9 billion.
The consolidation of new companies, especially Kemper Group of the U.S., accounted for about half of the gross premium growth.

In addition to the Kemper acquisition last year, Zurich Group acquired the Norwegian company Protector, it bought a majority stake in Seguros Sud America in Venezuela, received approvals for a second representive office in China and opened a laison office in India.
Hueppi said Zurich Group intends to remain on the expansion path and is especially keen to become a more important player in the global asset management business.
"We are strategically developing this new core business and plan to coordinate our expansion and utilise our existing resources on a global level," Hueppi said.
He said the group now has a solid base in the fund and asset management sector through its 1996 acquisition of Kemper Corp in the U.S.

At the end of 1996 the Zurich Kemper organisation had some 78 billion Swiss francs of investments under management. Of this total 60 billion were as mutual funds and 18 billion in institutional investments, Hueppi said.

Zurich is also planning to create authorised and conditional capital which could be used to move quickly should acquisition opportunities arise. However, the group said it had no specific plans to increase its share capital at this time.
Zurich will ask shareholders on June 11 to approve the creation of authorised capital of no more than 25 million Swiss francs, corresponding to a maximum of 2.5 million new shares.
It will also propose the creation of contingent capital of 35 million francs, or 3.5 million shares, of which one million shares will be reserved for employee share ownership plans.

"Acceptance of this proposal would give Zurich the necessary flexibility to issue additional shares or raise equity, which, for example, could be an important factor in the further expansion of our organisation," Hueppi said.
In addition, Zurich is making internal preparations for a possible listing in the U.S. and is likely to make a decision in mid-1998 on a move to the New York Stock Exchange, Hueppi said.
"The preparation on this is underway...we are interested in a global spread of shareholders," he said.
He said the plan calls for the company to report 1998 results according to the GAP (General Accounting Principles) required for listing in the U.S.
